Laboratory observations of Cuthona nana maintained at a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] reveal key early life-history parameters. Embryogenesis proceeds rapidly under these thermal conditions, with hatching occurring approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] after oviposition, yielding tiny planktotr at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]ophic veligers. The wet weight at birth of these newly hatched larvae is remarkably low, calculated to be 0.000002145 grams [Wwb = 0.000002145 grams], a value consistent with the extremely small egg diameter of approximately 160 micrometers typical of many aeolid nudibranchs. The free-swimming veliger stage persists for a substantial duration, with the time since birth at larval metamorphosis recorded as 80 days since birth  at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This extended planktonic phase allows for considerable dispersal potential within the water column before settlement and transformation into a benthic juvenile.

As juveniles grow, their developmental trajectory is tightly linked to body size thresholds. Metamorphosis from the veliger larva into the initial post-metamorphic juvenile occurs at a total length of just 0.5 centimeters , marking a critical point in morphological transformation. Thereafter, the growing juveniles continue to increase in size, and sexual maturation is initiated upon reaching a total length at puberty of approximately 1 centimeter [Lp = approximately 1 centimeter]. This threshold size, falling within a narrow range of 0.9 to 1.1 centimeters, appears to be a reliable indicator of gonadal development commencement. The time since birth at which this pubertal length is attained has been estimated at 90 days [tp = 90 days] under the standard laboratory conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], indicating a relatively rapid progression from metamorphosis to reproductive competence in this species.

The ultimate adult body size of Cuthona nana has been documented from both field collections and laboratory rearing studies. The ultimate total length typically reaches 2.3 centimeters [Li = 2.3 centimeters], although some marine life resources suggest a slightly larger maximum value of 2.8 centimeters, possibly reflecting geographic variation or differences in food availability. Corresponding to this adult length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual is estimated at approximately 0.14 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.14 grams], a modest body mass that is energetically efficient for a small, active predator of hydroids. This combination of relatively small size and low mass is typical of many aeolid nudibranchs, allowing them to exploit microhabitats on their sessile prey colonies with ease. The energetic demands of such a small body are correspondingly low, but the costs of reproduction must be carefully balanced against the limited lifespan.

Reproductive output in Cuthona nana was quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at the species' preferred temperature. At a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], it was determined that a single reproductive event involves the production of approximately 400 eggs per spawn [N_R_i = approximately 400 eggs per spawn]. Furthermore, individual adults are capable of spawning at a frequency of roughly 4.5 times per week [F_R_i = roughly 4.5 times per week]. This sustained high level of reproductive activity, achieved at this relatively cool temperature, is noteworthy and suggests a strategy of high fecundity to counteract potential high larval mortality in the plankton. The combination of a large clutch size and frequent spawning events results in a substantial investment in offspring production throughout the adult phase, ensuring that a sufficient number of larvae are released to maintain the population.

The overall longevity of Cuthona nana is constrained under the thermal conditions typical of its habitat. In our laboratory cultures held at a constant 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan from hatching to natural death was 125 days [am = 125 days]. This short life cycle, encompassing approximately four months, is characteristic of a semelparous or rapidly iteroparous life-history strategy common among small-bodied nudibranchs. Since embryogenesis is completed in 20 days [ab = 20 days], the entire developmental timeline from egg to reproductive adult can be compressed into a few months, allowing the species to complete multiple generations within a single favorable season at a temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This rapid turnover allows populations to respond quickly to resource pulses, with new generations potentially spawning within three months of their own birth. The brief lifespan also places a premium on early and efficient reproduction, favoring the high fecundity and frequent spawning we have documented.
